newsitem.title: UK: Study puts in doubt existence of "nearby" planets.
newsitem.headline: Study puts in doubt existence of "nearby" planets.

text.p: Evidence taken widely to show that planets may be orbiting nearby stars may in fact indicate no such thing, a Canadian astronomer said on Wednesday.

In a report sure to dismay the astronomical establishment, John Gray of the University of Western Ontario questioned whether astronomers in Geneva were correct in their claim to have found the first planet outside our solar system in 1995.
A first step towards finding life outside this solar system would be finding a planet like Earth orbiting another star.

Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz of the Geneva Observatory used measurements of the star 51 Pegasi, 40 light-years away in the constellation Pegasus, to show it was "wobbling" and argued this effect was caused by the gravitational pull of a large, orbiting planet.
But Gray took similar spectral images and said they could be natural variations in the radiation coming from the star.
"The presence of a planet is not required to explain the data," Gray wrote in a report in the science journal Nature.

No one can actually see the "planets", so what astronomers do is measure radiation coming from other stars. They can analyse it to show the mass of the stars, the speed at which they are travelling and their chemical make-up.

The analysis has also been interpreted to indicate that about nine stars outside the solar system have planets orbiting them. The idea is that the gravitational force of the planets causes "wobbles" in the radiation from the stars.
Gray said his measurements indicated the wobbles in 51 Pegasi's light were just natural fluctuations.
"Although at this stage the cause of the spectral line variations in 51 Pegasi are not fully understood, the chance of their being caused by a planet is vanishingly small," he wrote.
Gray's paper is sure to send astronomers and physicists back to their telescopes.
